tasks.title: Install boto3 inside a virtual environment for a new project.
Create a client and make one call that lists something small in your account.
Confirm boto3 finds your credentials the same way the AWS CLI does, with no keys in the code.
Create a client for a specific region rather than relying on the default.
Make one call each to two different services in the same script.
Run the same query with the AWS CLI and with boto3, and compare the two outputs.
Print the raw response and identify the outer keys before touching the data.
Reach a value nested two levels deep, using the skills from day 85.
Handle a key that may not be present rather than assuming it is always there.
Find out what happens when a result set is larger than one response.
Use a paginator to collect every result across all pages.
Print the total number of items found across every page.
Break it: call something your role cannot do and read the exception carefully.
Catch the AWS client error specifically rather than catching everything.
Extract the error code from the exception and act differently for two different codes.
Write a script that lists running instances with id, type and state.
Use a filter so the call returns only the instances you want, rather than filtering afterwards.
Pull the Name tag out of the tag list and print it alongside each instance.
Write a function that turns an AWS tag list into a plain Python dictionary.
Find every instance missing a required tag such as owner or project.
Print a report of untagged resources and exit non zero if any were found.
List your buckets with their creation dates.
List the objects in one bucket, handling pagination properly.
Calculate the total size of a bucket and print it in a readable unit.
Upload a file to a bucket from Python.
Download it again to a different name and confirm the contents match.
Write a function that checks whether an object exists without downloading it.
List every IAM user in the account.
Calculate the age of each access key using the date skills from day 101.
Compare this script to your bash version from day 55 and note which was easier to write.
Fetch CPU utilisation for one instance over the last hour.
Calculate the average from the returned datapoints.
Change the time range using datetime rather than hardcoded strings.
List your CloudWatch log groups with their retention settings.
Find any log group with no retention set and flag it as a cost risk.
Read recent log events from one group and print them.
Fetch your month to date spend from Python.
Break the spend down by service and print the top five.
Format the amounts to two decimal places with the currency shown.
Choose one check from your day 73 bash audit tool, such as open security groups.
Rewrite it in Python using boto3.
Make the output format match your bash tool so both can be used together.
Rewrite a second check, such as public buckets or unattached volumes.
Compare the bash and Python versions side by side and write down what changed.
Write your own rule for when to reach for bash and when to reach for Python.
Create the project with a main file, a checks module and a requirements file.
Add argparse with flags for region, profile and which checks to run.
Set up logging with levels rather than printing everything.
Write each check as a function that returns findings rather than printing them.
Give every finding the same shape: severity, resource, and a message.
Run every check and collect all findings into one list.
Print a readable report grouped by severity.
Add a flag that outputs the findings as JSON instead, for other tools to consume.
Exit non zero when any high severity finding is present.
Confirm the audit tool only reads and can never change anything.
For any cleanup feature, make dry run the default and require a flag to act.
Require an explicit confirmation before anything is deleted, as you did in bash.
Write two tests using fake responses rather than calling AWS.
Write a README covering what each check does, the flags, and the exit codes.
Commit it and note in your notes that this is the strongest Python thing you have built.

questions.prompt: What is boto3?
options: The Python library for working with AWS
questions.explanation: It is an API client, exactly like the one you built on day 119.

questions.prompt: Where does boto3 find your credentials?
options: The same places the AWS CLI looks, such as the credentials file and environment
questions.explanation: That is why you should never put keys in your Python code.

questions.prompt: Why specify a region explicitly in your code?
options: So the script cannot act in whichever region happens to be default
questions.explanation: Same reasoning as naming the profile explicitly in your bash scripts.

questions.prompt: What shape does a boto3 response usually have?
questions.explanation: It is JSON turned into Python data, which is why day 85 mattered.

questions.prompt: What should you do before writing code against a response?
options: Print the raw response and read its actual shape
questions.explanation: Assuming the shape is the fastest way to write code that breaks on the first real call.

questions.prompt: How should you handle a key that may not exist in a response?
options: Access it safely with a default
questions.explanation: Optional fields are common, and a KeyError in production is avoidable.

questions.prompt: What happens when a result set is larger than one response?
options: The response is truncated and you must page through the rest
questions.explanation: Missing this is how scripts silently report only the first page of results.

questions.prompt: What does a paginator do?
options: Handles fetching every page for you
questions.explanation: It removes the manual loop you would otherwise write yourself.

questions.prompt: Why is silently reading only the first page dangerous in an audit tool?
options: Because it reports a clean result while problems exist on later pages
questions.explanation: A tool that misses findings is worse than one that reports none, because it is trusted.

questions.prompt: Which exception should you catch for AWS API failures?
options: The specific AWS client error type
questions.explanation: Catching everything hides bugs, as you learned on day 90.

questions.prompt: Why extract the error code from an AWS exception?
options: Because different codes need different responses, such as retry versus fail
questions.explanation: Access denied and rate exceeded call for completely different handling.

questions.prompt: Why is boto3 easier to learn after building your own API client?
options: Because you already understand clients, pagination and error handling
questions.explanation: That was the entire reason day 119 came before this month.

questions.prompt: boto3 responses are nested Python dictionaries and lists.
questions.explanation: Everything you learned about nested data in Month 4 applies directly here.

questions.prompt: A script that only reads the first page of results is a common and silent bug.
questions.explanation: It looks like it works, which is exactly what makes it dangerous.

questions.prompt: Access keys should be written into Python code when the repository is private.
questions.explanation: boto3 finds credentials the same way the CLI does, and there is never a reason to embed them.

questions.prompt: Why use an API filter rather than fetching everything and filtering in Python?
options: Because less data is transferred and the call is faster
questions.explanation: Filtering at the source scales, and filtering afterwards does not.

questions.prompt: How are AWS tags returned in a response?
options: As a list of key and value pairs
questions.explanation: That is why converting them into a dictionary is one of the first helpers you write.

questions.prompt: Why write a helper that converts tags to a dictionary?
options: Because you will need it in every script that touches tags
questions.explanation: Small repeated conversions belong in one function, not in ten places.

questions.prompt: Why hunt for untagged resources?
options: Because cost allocation and cleanup both depend on tags
questions.explanation: An untagged resource is one nobody can attribute or safely delete.

questions.prompt: Why should a report tool exit non zero when it finds problems?
options: So it can be used as a gate in automation
questions.explanation: The same convention as your bash tools, which is what lets them work together.

questions.prompt: Why check whether an S3 object exists without downloading it?
options: Because downloading to check wastes time and transfer cost
questions.explanation: A metadata call answers the question far more cheaply.

questions.prompt: Why does listing objects in a large bucket need pagination?
options: Because the response is capped and returns only part of the list
questions.explanation: The same truncation problem, and the same paginator solution.

questions.prompt: How would you calculate the age of an access key?
options: Read it from the response directly
Compare its creation date to now using datetime
questions.explanation: This is exactly why dates came earlier in the track.

questions.prompt: Why was the IAM audit easier in Python than in bash?
options: Because dates, filtering and nested data are awkward in a shell pipeline
questions.explanation: Logic and data handling is where Python clearly wins over bash and jq.

questions.prompt: When is bash still the better choice?
options: Short glue work chaining a few commands together
questions.explanation: Bash remains excellent at gluing commands, and Python takes over when there is real logic.

questions.prompt: Why print sizes in a readable unit rather than raw bytes?
options: Because a human has to act on the number
questions.explanation: Usability decides whether you actually use your own tools.

questions.prompt: What should a required tag list be?
options: Configurable, so different projects can require different tags
questions.explanation: This is the configuration separated from code principle again.

questions.prompt: AWS tags come back as a list, not as a dictionary.
questions.explanation: Converting them is one of the small helpers that appears in almost every AWS script.

questions.prompt: Filtering in the API call is better than filtering after the response arrives.
questions.explanation: It reduces transfer, runs faster and scales to accounts with thousands of resources.

questions.prompt: Writing the same audit in bash and then in Python was wasted effort.
questions.explanation: Doing both is what teaches you which tool fits which job, which is a judgement employers value.

questions.prompt: What do CloudWatch metric calls return?
options: A list of datapoints over a time range
questions.explanation: You aggregate them yourself, which is the same as you did with jq in bash.

questions.prompt: Why use datetime rather than hardcoded time strings?
options: So the range moves with the current time instead of going stale
questions.explanation: A hardcoded date works today and silently breaks tomorrow.

questions.prompt: Why is a single datapoint a poor basis for a decision?
options: Because one value can be an outlier that means nothing
questions.explanation: Averages and trends are what tell you something real.

questions.prompt: Why flag a log group with no retention set?
options: Because logs kept forever quietly become a significant cost
questions.explanation: This is the same finding you built into your bash audit tool.

questions.prompt: Why format currency amounts to two decimal places?
options: Because raw floating point output is hard to read and looks unfinished
questions.explanation: Presentation matters for anything a human reads and acts on.

questions.prompt: Why break cost down by service rather than reporting a total?
options: Because the total does not tell you what to change
questions.explanation: You cannot reduce a cost you cannot locate.

questions.prompt: Why make your Python checks output the same format as your bash checks?
options: So both can be used together and read as one report
questions.explanation: Consistent interfaces are what let separate tools be combined.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of the Python version of an audit check?
options: Complex logic, dates and nested data are far easier to express
questions.explanation: Bash and jq get unreadable exactly where Python gets comfortable.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage the bash version keeps?
options: It is quicker to write for short glue work with no dependencies
questions.explanation: For three commands chained together, bash is still the right answer.

questions.prompt: Why write down your own rule for choosing between them?
options: Because making the choice deliberately beats defaulting to whichever you used last
questions.explanation: Engineers who can justify a tool choice are more useful than ones who only know one.

questions.prompt: What should you do when a boto3 call is rate limited?
questions.explanation: The same backoff pattern from bash day 48 and Python day 110.

questions.prompt: Why does reading logs from Python matter for later?
options: Because Month 8 builds real observability, and this is the manual version
questions.explanation: Doing it by hand once makes the managed tooling much easier to reason about.

questions.prompt: Hardcoded date strings in a monitoring script are a bug waiting to happen.
questions.explanation: The script works on the day you write it and silently reports nothing afterwards.

questions.prompt: Having written the same check twice, in bash and Python, gives you a real basis for choosing between them.
questions.explanation: Opinions about tools are much stronger when they come from having used both on the same problem.

questions.prompt: Python should replace bash entirely once you know it.
questions.explanation: Each is better at different work, and knowing when to use which is the actual skill.

questions.prompt: Why should each check return findings rather than print them?
options: So the caller decides how to display, filter or export them
questions.explanation: A function that prints cannot be reused, tested or reformatted.

questions.prompt: Why give every finding the same shape?
options: So they can be grouped, sorted and output in any format
questions.explanation: A consistent structure is what makes the JSON output possible at all.

questions.prompt: Why add a JSON output option?
options: So another tool or pipeline can consume the results
questions.explanation: Human readable and machine readable are both useful, for different readers.

questions.prompt: Why group the human readable report by severity?
options: So the reader deals with the most important findings first
questions.explanation: A flat list makes the reader do the prioritising, which they will not do.

questions.prompt: Why should an audit tool only read?
options: Because a tool that can change things can also break things while investigating
questions.explanation: Separating investigation from action limits the damage a bug can do.

questions.prompt: How should any cleanup feature behave by default?
options: Dry run, printing what it would remove
questions.explanation: Safe defaults with an explicit flag for action, exactly as in your bash tools.

questions.prompt: Why test with fake responses rather than real AWS calls?
options: Because tests must be fast, repeatable and not depend on the account state
questions.explanation: A test that depends on live infrastructure tells you nothing reliable.

questions.prompt: What should a README for this tool explain?
options: What each check does, the available flags, and what the exit codes mean
questions.explanation: Someone should be able to run it correctly without reading your code.

questions.prompt: Why does argparse matter for a tool with several checks?
options: Because users need to select regions, profiles and which checks to run
questions.explanation: Options are what turn a script into a tool other people can use.

questions.prompt: Why use logging levels rather than printing everything?
options: So normal output stays clean while detail is available when needed
questions.explanation: A tool that prints its internals by default is unusable in a pipeline.

questions.prompt: Why is this the strongest Python thing you have built so far?
options: Because it reads real infrastructure, handles failure, and produces actionable output
questions.explanation: It solves a real problem end to end, which is what makes a portfolio piece.

questions.prompt: What does this tool demonstrate to an employer?
options: That you understand what good and bad cloud configuration looks like
questions.explanation: You cannot write a check without knowing what it is checking for and why.

questions.prompt: A function that returns data is more reusable than one that prints it.
questions.explanation: Printing decides the output format for every caller, which is rarely what you want.

questions.prompt: An audit tool that can also delete resources is more useful and equally safe.
questions.explanation: Combining investigation with destruction means a bug during investigation can destroy things.

questions.prompt: This month was deliberately lighter because it falls during Ramadan.
questions.explanation: Both tracks were reduced together so the whole plan stays survivable rather than being abandoned.
